A menorah is a multi-branched candle holder (or oil lamp holder) that holds deep religious significance in Judaism. Think of it as a very special candlestick — but instead of holding just one candle, it holds several, arranged in a specific pattern that carries meaning.
The Two Types You Need to Know
The word "menorah" actually refers to two related but distinct objects. Understanding the difference is key to truly knowing this word.

This is the oldest and most sacred form. It has seven branches — a central stem with three branches curving out on each side, all at the same height. It held small cups of olive oil with wicks, not candles.

This menorah is described in the Hebrew Bible (the Torah) as something God commanded the ancient Israelites to build and keep burning inside their holy sanctuary — first in the Tabernacle (a portable tent-sanctuary they carried through the desert) and later in the great Temple in Jerusalem. It was never supposed to go out. It was tended by priests and burned continuously as a symbol of God's presence and light.

When the Roman Empire destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE, they reportedly took this golden menorah away as a trophy of conquest. This event is famously carved into the Arch of Titus, a monument still standing in Rome today, which shows Roman soldiers carrying the seven-branched menorah in a victory procession.

Because of this history, the seven-branched menorah became one of the most powerful and enduring symbols of the Jewish people — a symbol of their faith, identity, survival, and hope. It appears on the official emblem of the modern State of Israel.
2. The Nine-Branched Menorah — The Hanukkah Menorah (Also Called a Hanukkiah)

This is the menorah most people see and recognize today, especially in late November or December. It has nine branches — eight main ones plus one special branch called the shamash (a Hebrew word meaning "helper" or "servant").

It is used during Hanukkah, a Jewish festival that lasts eight nights. Each night of Hanukkah, one more candle is lit — one on the first night, two on the second, and so on until all eight are burning on the final night. The shamash is the candle used to light all the others and is kept slightly separate (usually placed higher or lower than the rest) so it's clearly distinct from the eight ritual candles.

Why eight candles? The story behind it: Around 165 BCE, a group of Jewish fighters called the Maccabees recaptured the Temple in Jerusalem from a Greek-Syrian empire that had desecrated it. When they went to rededicate the Temple and relight its menorah, they found only enough ritually pure olive oil to keep it burning for a single day. Yet, according to tradition, the oil miraculously burned for eight full days — exactly long enough for a new supply of oil to be prepared. Hanukkah (which means "dedication") commemorates this miracle. The nine-branched menorah, or hanukkiah, is a physical reenactment of that miracle, night by night.

The hanukkiah is traditionally placed in a window or doorway — the point is to display the light publicly, to proclaim the miracle to anyone passing by.
How the Word Is Used in Practice

In everyday speech, when someone says "menorah" — especially in the context of Hanukkah decorations, holiday displays, or gift shops — they almost always mean the nine-branched hanukkiah. This is the one you'll see in store windows in December, in photographs, and in news stories about Hanukkah celebrations.

Strictly speaking, however, "menorah" most precisely refers to the seven-branched Temple lamp, and "hanukkiah" is the technically correct term for the nine-branched Hanukkah version. Scholars and observant Jews often maintain this distinction, but in casual use, "menorah" has come to serve as a common shorthand for both — and especially for the hanukkiah.

A menorah is typically made of metal — historically gold or silver, today often brass, aluminum, or other materials. Some are simple and functional; others are ornate works of art. The branches curve upward, each ending in a cup or spike that holds a candle or oil wick. All the flames are meant to be at the same height (with the shamash being the exception in a hanukkiah). It is a recognizable, elegant object — symmetrical, flame-bearing, and immediately associated with Jewish identity and celebration.

The menorah — in both forms — is about light as a symbol of the divine, of hope, and of perseverance. The Temple menorah represented God's presence among the Jewish people. The hanukkiah represents the miracle of survival — a small group of people, a tiny amount of oil, holding on against overwhelming odds and lasting far longer than seemed possible. It is a symbol that has meant something to Jewish communities across thousands of years of history, across many countries and circumstances.

That combination — the sacred, the historical, the festive, and the deeply symbolic — is what the word "menorah" carries with it.
